newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS-Greece aims at EU convergence with 97 budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Greece aims at EU convergence with 97 budget.

text.p: Greece's 1997 austerity budget, unveiled on Friday, will put the European Union's poorest country within striking distance of joining the economic and monetary union, National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou said.
Greece took a step this year towards EMU, which Athens wants to join around 2001, and will "have covered five-sixths of the distance" if the 1997 budget is fully implemented, he said.
"Our first goal is ...to accelerate growth to 3.3 percent in 1997 from 2.6 percent in 1996," he told a news conference. "Our second goal is .. cutting the budget deficit."
Greece's convergence programme to align its economy with the rest of the EU forecasts GDP growth of 1.7 percent in 1996 and 2.6 percent in 1997.

The GDP breakdown showed that a high growth rate of 9.9 percent in real gross investment spending on fixed assets was mainly responsible for the real GDP growth of 2.6 percent in 1996. GDP growth was initially projected at 2.5 percent in 1995.
Real investment spending is expected to be the locomotive behind the 3.3 percent GDP growth in 1997.
The higher than planned GDP growth rates are instrumental in Greece's effort to help push the budget deficit to GDP and debt to GDP ratios down.

The ratios are among the criteria set out in the Maastricht treaty to bring EU economies together and lead to a single currency. The target date for EMU is 1999. Greece has said it hopes to be in a second group to enter in 2000 or 2001.
Greece's 1997 budget projects a general government budget deficit of 4.2 percent of GDP in 1997, down from 7.6 percent in 1996.
Revenues are projected to grow by 14.9 percent in 1997 from 12.8 percent in 1996, and expenditures to rise by 5.8 percent in 1997 against an expected 9.4 percent in 1996.

"An increase of 14.9 percent is a very ambitious target if it is taken into account that the nominal GDP is expected to increase by 10.4 percent in 1997," the introductory report with the budget said.
Average consumer price inflation is seen falling to 6.5 percent in 1997 from 8.5 percent in 1996, which would also entail a decrease in real spending next year.

"The reduction of inflation constitutes the cornerstone of our economic policy," Papandoniou said. "End-97 inflation of 4.5 percent is ambitious but necessary. Our long-term inflation goal is 3.0 percent."
Many bankers and brokers expect inflation to fall further in 1997 but considered the end-97 government figure implausible.
The central government primary surplus was projected to rise to 4.5 percent of GDP in 1997 from 2.4 percent in 1996 and 2.2 percent in 1995.

Primary surpluses from 1994 to 1996 and lower borrowing costs due to falling interest rates, drove down the general government to GDP ratio to 110.8 percent in 1996 from 111.7 percent in 1995. Maastricht calls for a ratio of 60 percent or lower.
Greece ranks third behind Belgium and Italy in terms of public debt to GDP ratio but has the highest interest payment to GDP ratio in the EU.
Interest payments on general government debt fell to 12.4 percent of GDP in 1996 from 12.9 percent in 1995.
"There was a decrease in real interest rates in 1996 that will contribute to the reduction of interest payments in 1997 and beyond," the budget report said.

Papandoniou said his third goal was social cohesion. He pointed to the heavier taxation of capital and high-income earners as well as to the freeze of indirect taxes in drachma terms and small increases in utility charges.
Organised labour and farmers have staged rallies and strikes around the country this week to protest against what Papandoniou has called "the toughest budget in 15 years".
